title: Why I'm posting for 20 days
post:
The last 4-5 months have been the most fun I’ve had building: 20 working AI products, from family care to disaster prediction.
For 20 days, I’ll break down one a day: the problem, trade-offs and live link.

What came out of it: live products across AI agents, family care, mental health, climate, education, sales, music, publishing and AR. Apps on Android and iPhone, 7 books on Amazon, and a music channel with 139 videos that runs at ₹0.

Before building full time, I spent close to 4 years at Times Internet, growing from APM to Senior PM:
• Led the discovery, registration and acquisition journeys for the inaugural Times Internet Delhi Half Marathon: 18K+ runners
• Launched paid wellness subscriptions for Times Health+
• Scaled The Economic Times’ Assisted Sales revenue from ₹15L to ₹80L a month, and built AI TeleSuite for that team
• Unlocked ₹3Cr+ in incremental annual revenue with the ET Markets web revamp

Most recently, I ran D2C growth across the US, UK and global markets.

My learnings:
1. AI made building fast. Deciding what’s worth building is still the hard part.
2. Writing the code is now the easy part. Making it work on every phone, every edge case and every bad network is the real work.
3. People forgive an AI that says “I’m not sure”. They don’t forgive one that’s confidently wrong.
4. If a new user doesn’t get value in the first minute, they won’t come back for a second visit.
5. Building a product is half the job. Getting people to use it is the other half, which is why I’m sharing all 20 here.

One more thing: from tomorrow, these posts go out through a publishing workflow I built, and on the last day I’ll show you how it works.

Follow along, and tell me in the comments which product you’re most curious about. And if you try one and hit a bug, DM me. Every report helps.

title: LifeCycle-OS
post:
Project 1/20: LifeCycle-OS. Enter any brand, get a full lifecycle marketing plan in seconds.
And unlike many AI tools, it refuses to make up a single price, rating or review.

The problem: D2C lifecycle teams have to ship emails, ads and landing pages for every cohort, every week. AI drafts them fast, but it also invents prices nobody set, ratings nobody earned and reviews nobody wrote, and a fast draft becomes a compliance issue after the send.

The insight: a confident wrong fact costs more than a visible blank.

What I built: LifeCycle-OS benchmarks a brand’s category, designs a complete lifecycle plan, then turns real customer data into on-brand mailers, ads and landing pages.

Key product decisions:
• Missing facts stay missing. They’re marked “DATA REQUIRED BEFORE LAUNCH” instead of being guessed.
• Brand isolation in code. One brand’s data can never appear in another brand’s campaign, and tests prove it on every change.
• Multi-brand from day one. Any brand onboards and the platform takes on its colours, voice and catalogue.

The trade-off: some drafts come out with gaps a human must fill. I chose that over silent errors.

How I’ll measure success: share of assets sent with zero factual errors, and time from brief to send.

💬 Your turn: Would you trust an AI that leaves a blank over one that guesses?

title: The Third Eye
post:
Project 2/20: The Third Eye, a personal AI operating system.
One assistant that works across your tasks, notes, goals, calendar and email, so you stop switching apps.

The problem: busy people run their day across too many apps. Tasks live in one, notes in another, email and calendar somewhere else, so no assistant ever sees the full picture.

The insight: people don’t need one more app. They need one assistant that can use the apps they already have.

What I built: an assistant that takes actions by voice and camera, and checks your personal knowledge base before it answers.

Key product decisions:
• Four assistant modes, each tuned for a different kind of work, so you switch the assistant’s style instead of switching apps.
• A hub, not a silo: 24 tools I built plus 76 linked apps.
• A business model from day one: credit packs paid through Razorpay.

The trade-off: I shipped a working product on a simpler architecture first. A fuller agent backend is built and tested, and deploys next.

How I’ll measure success: tasks completed through the assistant each week, and tools connected per user.

title: Parwah
post:
Project 3/20: Parwah, a family-care app for Indian families looking after ageing parents.
It ends the WhatsApp line every family knows: “I thought you did.”

The problem: siblings in different cities share their parents’ care through a family WhatsApp group. “Did anyone book Papa’s blood test?” Everyone sees the message. Nobody knows who’s handling it.

The insight: caring for parents is a task problem, not a chat problem.

What I built: Parwah (परवाह) answers three questions for every need: what does your parent need, who is handling it, and when is it done?

Key product decisions:
• Clear ownership. Every need moves from open, to assigned, to claimed, to done. One tap says “I’m on it”.
• Handing a task back is normal, not a failure. Anyone can reopen a task, and the full history is kept.
• Family-level permissions and a full history of who changed what, so everyone stays in the loop without stepping on each other’s toes.

The trade-off: a task board asks a little more of families than a chat. Clear ownership is worth that small step.

How I’ll measure success: needs closed per family each month, and how quickly an open need gets claimed.

title: LoosenUp
post:
Project 4/20: LoosenUp, a stress-relief app built for your worst 2 minutes, not your best 20.
Rate how calm you feel, take a short guided break, and see the difference it made.

The problem: when you’re tense or low, you need relief in the moment. But many wellness apps want a sign-up, a 20-minute session and a daily streak, and on your worst day you’ll do none of it.

The insight: design for the worst moment, not the average one.

What I built: a 2-minute guided break matched to what you’re carrying, with a before and after calm rating.

Key product decisions:
• Value you can see. You rate how calm you feel before and after, and see your “Calm gain”.
• Safety first. An SOS button on every screen, even before sign-up, with Tele-MANAS 14416, a trusted contact and emergency 112. Distress phrases typed anywhere bring help forward.
• No barriers. No account needed, it works offline, and it installs without an app store.

The trade-off: I chose short and simple over deep programmes. It’s a wellbeing companion, not medical care, and it says so.

How I’ll measure success: average Calm gain, and how many people come back within 7 days.

💬 Your turn: What do you do in the worst 2 minutes of your day?

title: Predict Natural Disasters
post:
Project 5/20: Predict Natural Disasters, a live global hazard map built on 8 official data sources.
Its best feature: it grades its own forecasts and tells you when it was wrong.

The problem: newsrooms, NGOs and operations teams need one trustworthy global view when disaster strikes, but the data is spread across a dozen agency websites. And many “AI predicts disasters” products make bold forecasts that nobody ever checks.

The insight: in a high-stakes field, being believed matters more than being impressive.

What I built: one live map combining USGS, NASA, GDACS, NOAA, EMSC, ReliefWeb and more, with experimental outlooks on top.

Key product decisions:
• Every forecast is accountable. Each one states its evidence, its confidence and the time window it will be graded in, then it’s checked against what actually happened.
• Failures stay small. If one source goes down, coverage shrinks, but the map never goes blank.
• Silence isn’t safety. If no source covers a region, it says “not covered”, never “all clear”.

The trade-off: fewer flashy predictions in exchange for more trust.

How I’ll measure success: forecast hit rate against the rules declared upfront, and coverage per source.

💬 Your turn: Would you rather have a bold forecast or an honest one?

title: Edu AI
post:
Project 6/20: Edu AI, an AI-first learning planner for a child’s whole education, from birth to Class 12.
Because today, no app a child uses knows what the last one taught.

The problem: from a toddler app to JEE coaching, an Indian child’s education passes through app after app, and each one starts from zero. Parents never get one clear plan from year to year.

The insight: learning is one continuous journey, so the product should track it as one.

What I built: one skill map aligned to NCERT and India’s National Curriculum Framework, from home learning at birth to Class 12. Competitive and study-abroad tracks branch from it, so nothing starts from zero.

Key product decisions:
• One map from age 0 to 18. JEE, NEET, CUET and UPSC tracks branch off it from Class 8-9.
• Grounded in India’s official curriculum frameworks, across CBSE, ICSE/ISC, NIOS and state boards.
• Zero screen time for children under 3. The product guides parents, not toddlers.

The trade-off: I built the data foundations before a single lesson, because in education the structure is the product.

How I’ll measure success: plans followed month after month, and how often parents come back to adjust them.

💬 Your turn: Parents: how many learning apps has your child used so far?

title: AI TeleSuite
post:
Project 7/20: AI TeleSuite, an AI toolkit that listens to every sales call so managers can coach.
I built it at The Economic Times, where I scaled Assisted Sales from ₹15L to ₹80L a month.

The problem: in a growing Assisted Sales team, call quality depends on coaching, and coaching depends on listening. A manager can only hear a handful of calls. The rest go unheard, unscored and uncoached.

The insight: let AI listen to every call, so managers can spend their time coaching.

What I built: one toolkit that transcribes every call, scores it, including how objections were handled, and helps agents with the pitch.

Key product decisions:
• Two versions in one product: a full version on paid AI services and a free open-source version, so it works on any budget.
• Built for internal use, with server-checked PIN access and a lockout, because call data is sensitive.
• Built inside the team that would use it. I didn’t guess at the problem. I lived it every day.

The trade-off: a PIN-locked internal tool is harder to demo publicly, but call data has to stay private.

How I measured it: share of calls reviewed, and conversion per agent, alongside the team’s revenue growth from ₹15L to ₹80L a month.

💬 Your turn: Sales leaders: how many of your team’s calls do you actually get to hear?

title: Hey Yaara
post:
Project 8/20: Hey Yaara, a Hinglish AI voice companion you can call like a friend.
“Yaar, aaj ka din bekaar tha.” Many AI assistants reply like a textbook. Yaara replies like a friend.

The problem: many voice assistants are built English-first. Many Indians talk in Hinglish, and an assistant that answers like a textbook feels like software, not company.

The insight: for a voice companion, the experience is the product. And the worst experience is silence.

What I built: a companion you “call” like a friend, in Hinglish by default, with a music hub and games for when you’d rather not talk.

Key product decisions:
• Familiar sign-up: a mobile number and PIN, the way Indians already sign up for apps. No email needed.
• Fallbacks everywhere. If the AI model fails, a backup takes over. If the premium voice fails, the phone’s own voice speaks. The call never goes quiet.
• Private by design. Every call and transcript belongs only to its account, and access is checked on every request.

The trade-off: building native apps took longer than the web version alone, but phones’ own speech engines make the call feel real.

How I’ll measure success: average call length, repeat calls each week and in-app ratings.

title: Animind
post:
Project 9/20: Animind, an AI that reads your pet’s state from a 10-second recording.
Not a “pet translator”. It tells you what the sound can actually reveal, and how sure it is.

The problem: pet owners can hear that something is wrong, but not what kind of wrong. And “AI pet translators” promise to decode words that animals don’t use.

The insight: an animal’s sound reliably carries two signals: arousal (how worked up it is) and valence (distressed or happy), read from features like pitch contour and jitter. Build on what’s real, not what sounds magical.

What I built: record 10 seconds, and Animind gives a plain sentence, the measurements behind it and an honest confidence level.

Key product decisions:
• Clear positioning: not a translator, not a diagnosis.
• If a recording is too noisy, it says so instead of guessing.
• It compares against what’s normal for the species and for your own animal.

The trade-off: modest, honest answers over magical ones that would go viral and then lose trust.

How I’ll measure success: repeat recordings per pet, and how often vets find the readings useful.

title: TH+ LifeEngine
post:
Project 10/20: TH+ LifeEngine, an AI planner for personalised yoga and food plans.
Ask an AI chatbot for a diet plan and you usually get a paragraph. You can’t track a paragraph.

The problem: people want a yoga and nutrition plan they can follow, log and adjust. AI gives them nice text, but an app can’t schedule, track or update a paragraph.

The insight: AI output only becomes a product feature once it’s structured and checked.

What I built: a planner whose plans arrive as structured data, so they show up as daily meal checklists with macros (protein, carbs, fat, fibre) and timed yoga sessions, not a wall of chat text.

Key product decisions:
• A fixed plan format the app can read. Anything else is rejected.
• Two AI steps: one drafts the plan, a second checks it.
• Built from real lists of yoga sequences and foods, not made-up options.
• The optional AI coach sits behind an on/off switch to keep costs under control.

The trade-off: strict structure limits how creative the AI can be. Reliability wins.

How I’ll measure success: plans followed past week one, and days logged per user.

title: Markets Pro
post:
Project 11/20: Markets Pro, a trading research engine for India, the US, China and Russia.
Its demo loses money on purpose, and that’s the most honest thing about it.

The problem: retail investors want strategies they can trust before risking real money, but many backtests show beautiful profit curves that quietly cheat. They peek at future prices (look-ahead bias), ignore taxes or skip settlement rules, and real money pays for the bug.

The insight: the product isn’t trade ideas. It’s numbers you can trust.

What I built: a research engine that tests long-term momentum and short-term swing strategies with each market’s real rules and costs.

Key product decisions:
• Real costs per market: STT, stamp duty and GST in India, regulatory fees in the US, T+1 settlement in China.
• Every calculation is checked against hand-worked answers. One failure blocks the release.
• Paper trading only, with no broker connection. Trust comes before money.

The trade-off: the demo runs on random data, so after realistic costs it should lose. If it made a profit, that would prove a bug.

How I’ll measure success: a paper-trading track record on real market data, before any real money is involved.

💬 Your turn: Have you ever trusted a backtest that turned out too good to be true?

title: MuseVibe Studio
post:
Project 12/20: MuseVibe Studio, an AI music studio that turns a one-line idea into a full song.
Many AI music tools give you one text box and hope. This one helps you say what you mean.

The problem: many people know how a song should feel, but not the words for it: genre, tempo, vocal style, studio effects. So they type one vague line and get a random result.

The insight: people know the feeling, not the vocabulary. The product should translate.

What I built: describe your idea in plain words, like “a late-night drive in the Mumbai rain after a breakup”, and MuseVibe fills in the genre, tempo, mood, vocals and lyrics, ready to refine and generate.

Key product decisions:
• One line in, every field filled: genre, mood, energy, vocals and lyrics.
• AI help on every field, with Suggest and Enhance, so you can push one detail without starting over.
• Lyrics that respect language, including natural mixes like Hinglish.
• A single song or a full album, with a matching visual video if you want one.

The trade-off: more fields on screen than a single text box, but every one is optional and pre-filled.

How I’ll measure success: songs completed per session, and how often people refine instead of starting over.

💬 Your turn: If you could make a song from one line, what would it be about?

title: Kolab
post:
Project 13/20: Kolab, a two-sided platform for creators and the brands that pay them.
Brands stop paying for follower counts and pay on results from verified creators.

The problem: Indian creators run their business across a pile of apps, and brands still can’t tell which creators are real, so they pay for follower counts instead of results.

The insight: both sides have the same problem. The tools and the trust live in different places.

What I built: creators plan and schedule content, link every channel, launch a coupon storefront with affiliate codes and get paid. Brands discover verified creators and run commission deals.

Key product decisions:
• Two-sided pricing: creators subscribe to Basic or Pro, brands partner on commission.
• Verification is the moat. Linked channels make a creator trustworthy to a brand.
• Built for India: mobile OTP and Aadhaar eKYC sign-in are designed in and run in demo mode until a licensed KYC partner is plugged in.

The trade-off: prototype first. I’m proving the flow before paying for the expensive parts.

How I’ll measure success: verified creators onboarded, and brand deals closed per creator.

title: Shoutout
post:
Project 14/20: Shoutout, one platform for independent musicians to find gigs, collaborators and auditions.
Every request becomes a “Shout” that someone answers, and that one idea runs the whole platform.

The problem: independent musicians find gigs in one place, collaborators in DMs and auditions somewhere else, and payment is informal at best.

The insight: underneath every interaction is the same action. Someone asks, someone answers.

What I built: one platform where every request, from a gig to a collab to an audition, is a Shout.

Key product decisions:
• One unit, many uses. 12 types of Shout are set up as configuration, so a new type doesn’t mean a new product.
• One matching engine for every type, so recommendations improve across the platform.
• Payments on double-entry accounting, because marketplaces die when payments break.
• Humans review auditions and disputes, where judgement matters.

The trade-off: a general building block takes longer to design than a single gig board, but the platform can grow without being rebuilt.

How I’ll measure success: Shouts answered within 48 hours, and repeat bookings.

title: ANCHOR
post:
Project 15/20: ANCHOR, an AI techno artist that releases a new track every single day.
It runs on an automated pipeline I built, around the clock, at ₹0.

The problem: an artist needs a steady stream of releases to grow an audience, and creators rarely fail for lack of talent. They fail at consistency.

The insight: consistency can be automated, as long as quality and platform rules are built in.

What I built: every day, ANCHOR writes a creative brief, generates an industrial techno track, checks its quality, masters it, designs the cover, cuts a Short, publishes everywhere with AI disclosure, and updates its website. Every Sunday it releases a weekly mix.

Key product decisions:
• Zero cost as a constraint. Free compute and open-source models shaped the whole design.
• Quality gates check loudness (LUFS), clipping and tempo, so silent or broken tracks never ship.
• Built for platform rules. Every release changes tempo, key, sound, cover and visuals.
• Failure you can see. If a run breaks, the status turns red, and nothing posts twice.

Where it publishes:
• YouTube @ANCHOR_AT: 139 videos so far, with 25 subscribers and growing
• Instagram @anchor_at2803: every release as a Reel

The trade-off: zero cost means slower free models, so each release takes longer to make.

Results so far: 139 videos published, at ₹0.

title: JobHunt
post:
Project 16/20: JobHunt, a free AI agent that finds real job openings and tailors your resume to each one.
Without ever inventing experience you don’t have.

The problem: job hunting means endless open tabs and one resume sent everywhere. Tailoring each application takes hours, and many AI tools exaggerate to fill the gaps.

The insight: the hard part isn’t finding openings. It’s tailoring each application without exaggerating.

What I built: sign in with Google and search once. JobHunt pulls real openings from free public job boards, links one-click searches on LinkedIn, Indeed, Glassdoor and Upwork, and writes a tailored resume and cover letter for each job.

Key product decisions:
• Grounded only in what you give it. It matches your real experience to each job’s keywords and never invents any.
• Your profile stays in your own browser, not on my servers.
• Free, with no API key and no setup.

The trade-off: free public job boards have fewer listings than paid feeds, but every listing is real.

How I’ll measure success: applications sent per session, and interviews per application.

title: Books on Amazon
post:
Project 17/20: a book publishing engine. 4 thrillers and 3 kids’ drawing books, now on Amazon.
Written with an engine I built, and published in every format.

The problem: I wanted to test whether one person, with AI, can run a real publishing business. Publishing usually takes writers, editors, designers and months per book, and many self-published AI books are low quality and get ignored.

The insight: AI can do the volume, but only quality gates make it a real product.

What I built:
• The Watermark Files: an Indian conspiracy-thriller series under my own name. Books 1-4: The Palace Writer, The Stamp Vendor, The Second Inventory and The Devpur Deed. Lead: Ira Sahni, a document examiner from Delhi.
• Doodle Lane Studio: step-by-step drawing books for kids 6-9 (Christmas, cute animals, and things that go), promoted with a new drawing every day on Instagram @ai_at2803.

Key product decisions:
• A series, not one-offs. A recurring lead brings readers back for the next book.
• Quality gates: originality and plagiarism checks, plain-English style rules, and a chain of AI models so drafting never stalls.
• Every format, every store: Kindle, paperback and hardcover. Book 1 is ₹99 so new readers can try the series.

Results so far: 7 books live on Amazon, and a new drawing Reel every day on @ai_at2803.

The trade-off: zero ad spend means slower discovery. I’m growing it organically first.

title: The Passion Table
post:
Project 18/20: The Passion Table, a daily home-style food service run from neighbourhood kitchens.
Subscribe, order on demand or reserve a table, so nobody at home has to be the one who cooks.

The problem: in working households in Indian cities, dinner means cooking after work, a cook who didn’t turn up, or another ₹400 delivery you regret by 9 PM. And the assumption that one person in the house, usually a woman, will handle it.

The insight: restaurant food is a treat. Daily food needs to be home-style, reliable and decided once.

What I built: the product end to end. Local “Eating Joints” cook fresh every day, and you choose how the food reaches you. It isn’t taking public orders yet.

Key product decisions:
• Three ways to eat from one kitchen: a meal subscription, on-demand ordering with live tracking, or a reserved table.
• Choice without the daily decision. Subscribers pick one of three meals each day, and can pause, resume or change any time.
• Home-style, not restaurant-style: food built to be eaten five nights a week.

The trade-off: this is the only product on this list with real-world operations, which makes it slower to scale than software.

How I’ll measure success: subscriber retention month on month, and on-time deliveries.

title: Airpane
post:
Project 19/20: Airpane, an AR browser that makes any website float in your room.
No headset and no app. Just the phone, laptop and TV you already own.

The problem: AR headsets cost more than many phones, and many people will never buy one.

The insight: the hardware for AR is already in people’s pockets: a phone camera and a laptop webcam.

What I built: on a phone, the page stays pinned in your room. On a laptop, the webcam tracks your head so the page looks like a 3D hologram. On a TV, it catches pages you throw to it.

Key product decisions:
• A gesture people already know: pinch, swing and let go to throw a page to your TV. Your phone becomes the remote.
• No app needed on any device, including iPhones and smart TVs.
• Sites that block embedding open in a cloud browser that only switches on when enabled, so costs stay in check.

The trade-off: browser-based AR is less precise than a headset, but it reaches everyone.

How I’ll measure success: pages thrown to a TV per session, and return visits.

title: Portfolio and Anchit LLM
post:
Project 20/20: my portfolio, with an AI that answers questions about my work in my own voice.
Don’t just read about my work. Question it.

The problem: people want to understand what someone has built, quickly and in depth, but a portfolio page can’t answer follow-up questions.

The insight: treat the portfolio as a product, with the visitor as the user.

What I built: “Anchit LLM”, an assistant grounded only in my real work, which answers questions in a cloned version of my voice.

Key product decisions:
• Grounded only in real material, so it can’t invent achievements.
• Voice streamed in short chunks, so it starts talking almost instantly. Waiting kills curiosity.
• Works everywhere: the web, an installable app on your phone and a TV.

The trade-off: a voice assistant is more to build than a static page, but it lets people try my work, not just read about it.

How I’ll measure success: questions asked per visit, and the conversations it starts.

title: The workflow behind the series
post:
You’ve just read 20 product stories in 20 days. I didn’t publish a single one of them by hand.
Here’s the workflow that did, and why I built it.

The problem: builders ship, then go quiet. Writing about your work can take as long as building it, so many projects never get their story told.

The insight: automate the repetitive part, and keep a human exactly where trust lives.

What I built: a publishing workflow that keeps my approved posts in a private queue and publishes the next one at 9 AM, using LinkedIn’s official API.

The product decisions:
• Publish only. It never likes, comments on others’ posts, messages or connects. Every conversation stays human.
• A content guard checks every post before it goes out. Unfinished placeholders or broken formatting block it.
• I approve every post before it goes live.
• Built for failure. It never posts twice, a pause switch stops everything, and if a run breaks I get an email and the next day carries on.

It’s built the same way as ANCHOR, my automated pipeline that releases a techno track every day.

The lesson: automation shouldn’t replace your voice. It should make sure you actually use it.

That’s the series. If one of these products sparked an idea, tell me in the comments or send me a DM. I read every one.
